Franklin Delano Roosevelt. On January 6, 1941, nine months before Pearl Harbor, he addressed Congress and articulated four freedoms as the universal aspirations at stake in the looming global conflict. The speech reframed the war as a contest for fundamental human rights.

Roosevelt enumerated these freedoms: freedom of speech and expression, freedom of worship, freedom from want, and freedom from fear. He framed them not as American luxuries but as universal values, things for which all peoples in all lands were fighting. As Americans, he said, we are not afraid of this future. Notably, he emphasized that the freedoms included protection from want—suggesting economic security as a human right, not mere charity.

The Four Freedoms became iconographic. Norman Rockwell created four paintings illustrating them, further embedding the vision in American culture. The speech helped justify Lend-Lease aid to Britain and the Soviet Union, framing economic and military support as defense of universal principles. Roosevelt's vision shaped the postwar liberal world order and the very founding of the United Nations, making these freedoms central to the international institutions that would follow.
